Photograph: supplied New South Wales Yvonne Whear’s car found in river as mystery surrounding NSW woman’s disappearance continues Police say personal items thought to belong to Whear recovered from waterlogged vehicle Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Susan Chenery Tue 15 Sep 2026 20.11 EDT Last modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 22.17 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A car belonging to missing woman Yvonne Whear has been found in northern New South Wales , about seven months since the 73-year-old was last seen. Police divers found the car in the Rous River in Dulguigan on Saturday 12 September – a short distance from Whear’s home. Police confirmed the vehicle had undergone forensic investigation – the mechanics of the vehicle were also under examination. Yvonne Whear vanished from a NSW town. Her daughter believes some people aren’t talking Read more “Several personal items, believed to belong to Yvonne, were also recovered,” police said in a statement. “Yvonne was not located with the vehicle and remains outstanding as a missing person.” View image in fullscreen Yvonne Whear was last seen on CCTV on 19 February buying orange juice and putting $50 credit on her phone. Photograph: supplied Whear’s family said they were devastated by her disappearance and expressed deep gratitude to “Sun State Search, our dedicated team of volunteers, NSW water police, the specialist police dive team, Tweed Heads police, and the local recovery services who assisted with the operation”. Whear was last seen on CCTV on 19 February buying orange juice and putting $50 credit on her phone at the Shell service station in Murwillumbah, before she drove out through the cane fields to her small hobby farm at the hamlet of Dungay. She had lived there for 23 years with a menagerie of the animals she cared for. At 8.30pm a member of the public reported seeing the car, a gold Ford Escape wagon, parked in the dark without lights, on Dungay Creek Road, less than a kilometre from where she lived. Map showing Yvonne Whear’s last known movements in and around Murwillumbah, northern NSW. Map showing Yvonne Whear’s last known movements in and around Murwillumbah, northern NSW. Her daughter Gillian Hallac said that she never drove at night if she could help it. Her boots and hat that she had been wearing in the CCTV footage were still in her house, she had food in the slow cooker, her usual shoes were at the door. Her clothes were folded on her bed ready for the next day. Her family said she would never leave her animals, even for one night. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion Her phone last pinged at 10am the next morning from a tower that put her phone in the area where her car was found on Saturday. View image in fullscreen Police said there was no evidence to suggest Yvonne Whear would voluntarily disappear. Photograph: supplied Hallac, who was in constant communication with her mother, says there was nothing to indicate anything was wrong. She didn’t suffer depression, she wasn’t on medication, and didn’t have mental health issues. “She’s the type of person who would let you know if she was unhappy,” Hallac told the Guardian in August. Dept acting insp Chris Elliott, Tweed-Byron district’s crime manager, said there was no evidence to suggest Yvonne would voluntarily disappear. Hallac has said she believed someone may have taken Whear and hidden her car. “That is my belief based on what I know about the circumstances in which she disappeared.” Explore more on these topics New South Wales news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://praguemonitor.com/pm/housing-dev.text: Czechia Business Prague Housing Europe & World Work & Life Briefings Key points Foreign individuals can generally own flats and houses in Czechia, and ownership is recorded in the public Cadastre of Real Estate. Agricultural land, forests and purchases through companies follow separate rules, and sanctions law can bar particular buyers. The practical hurdles are Czech-language paperwork, anti-money-laundering checks and the land registry filing, not a ban on foreign owners. On this page 7 sections What the law actually distinguishes Where the exceptions are The practical hurdles Buying from abroad Residence is a separate question Costs and timing A first step Yes, and for a long time. A foreign national does not need a residence permit, a Czech partner or a special licence to buy a flat in Prague. The question that fills expat forums is therefore usually the wrong one. The useful question is not "am I allowed?" but "what exactly am I buying, who is on the other side, and can I get the paperwork through a Czech office that works entirely in Czech?" The confusion has understandable roots. Rules on land have differed over the years, and a rumour about farmland easily becomes a rumour about everything. Add the volume of documents a purchase involves, and a procedural headache starts to feel like a legal bar. It is not one. The short answer For a flat, a house or a commercial unit, a foreign individual follows the same procedure as a Czech buyer. The exceptions sit with land, companies and sanctions, and the hurdles are practical. What the law actually distinguishes Czech property law draws its main line between kinds of property and kinds of buyer, not between citizens and foreigners. An apartment in a residential block is a unit ( jednotka ), registered as a separate object. A family house is a building on a parcel. A shop or office is a commercial unit. A foreign individual who buys any of these signs a written contract, and the new owner is then entered in the Cadastre of Real Estate ( katastr nemovitostí ), kept by the Czech Office for Surveying, Mapping and Cadastre (ČÚZK). For buyers from the EU the position is straightforward in practice. For buyers from outside the EU, residential property is open too, but exceptions are scattered across several laws, and a short check with a Czech lawyer is cheap insurance. The check is not there because the answer is probably "no". It is there because the lawyer will also tell you which documents the registry will want from a buyer in your position. Where the exceptions are What you are buying matters more than who you are Purchase Position Who to ask Flat, house or commercial unit, bought personally Same procedure as for a Czech buyer A Czech lawyer, for the paperwork Agricultural land and forests Separate rules; restrictions have varied with the buyer and the use of the land A lawyer, before any offer Purchase through a company Possible, but it changes the legal and tax picture A lawyer and a tax adviser together Buyer or seller on a sanctions list Cannot freely buy or sell; banks, notaries and lawyers screen for it The professional handling the deal As of 2026; check the official source. This table describes principles, not a ruling on any particular case. Agricultural land and forests are the area where old rumours come from. The rules follow the buyer and the way the land is used, and what applies to a flat does not apply to a field. A newcomer buying a weekend plot with a cottage should expect the parcel details to matter, because land registered as farmland and land registered as a building plot are different things in law and in tax. It is not a sensible first purchase. Buying through a company is possible. A foreign person can own a Czech company, and the company can own property. People are often drawn to this by the idea that it simplifies matters for a non-resident. It does the opposite: it adds a second legal entity, accounting duties and a different tax position. It is a decision for a lawyer and a tax adviser, not a shortcut around a form. Sanctions apply to property transactions like any other. A sanctioned person cannot freely buy or sell, and banks, notaries and lawyers are obliged to screen for it. The screening covers sellers as well as buyers, so an unusually quick offer on an unusually cheap flat from an unfamiliar seller is a reason for more checks, not fewer. The practical hurdles The law is the easy part. The land registry works in Czech, so documents issued abroad generally need a sworn translation by a court-appointed translator, and some need additional certification before a Czech office will accept them. If you are buying from outside the country, allow weeks for this rather than days. A birth certificate or a company extract that arrives without the right stamp is a classic cause of delay. Anti-money-laundering rules apply too. A bank, notary, lawyer or estate agent may ask where the money comes from, and they are obliged to. It is routine and Czechs get the same questions, but a non-resident with funds in a foreign account meets them more often and with more paperwork behind them. Have bank statements and the documents behind your funds ready before you sign, not after the notary asks. Buying from abroad You do not have to be in Prague on the day. Some buyers sign through a representative holding a power of attorney. The document must be in the right form for a property transaction, usually with officially verified signatures, and it is exactly where a small mistake can sink the registry filing. A template found on a forum is not the answer. Have a Czech lawyer or notary prepare it, and have it checked against the draft contract so that the representative is authorised to do precisely what the contract says. Think, too, about who will collect the paperwork afterwards. The registry decision, the handover protocol and the first annual tax return all need someone with a Czech address or at least a reliable contact. Many foreign owners solve this with a lawyer or an accountant. Few solve it by hoping for the best. Before you fall for a particular flat Look at the register Open the free online view of the Cadastre on the ČÚZK website and search for any address. Learn what an ownership record looks like. Ask what the seller is A private person, a couple, a company or an estate each bring different paperwork. Ask early. List your own documents Passport, proof of address, proof of funds, and any foreign documents that will need sworn translation. Book an hour with a lawyer Choose one who works with foreign buyers and ask for a written list of what they would need from you. Residence is a separate question Owning a flat does not give you the right to live in Czechia. Residence permits for non-EU citizens are handled by the Ministry of the Interior, and a purchase does not create a right of stay on its own. EU citizens have their own registration rules for longer stays. Buyers who plan to move here should treat the two tracks as independent: the flat can be bought in weeks, and the permit has its own timetable and its own requirements. The reverse also holds. Having a residence permit does not make a purchase simpler in law. It helps in practice, because a resident has a Czech address, a Czech bank account and usually a Czech phone number, which is how many small procedural frictions disappear. Costs and timing Nothing extra is charged for being foreign. You pay what everyone pays: the land registry fee, any broker or legal fees, and the annual property tax that falls on the owner. Our separate pieces cover each of these. How a non-resident is taxed, including in the home country, is a question for a qualified adviser (as of 2026; check the official source with the Financial Administration). Timing depends mostly on the registry. Applications are processed in order, and once the entry is made, the buyer is the owner with effect from the day the application arrived. That is the moment the whole procedure is built around, and our piece on the land registry explains it. Frequently asked questions Do I need a residence permit to buy a flat in Czechia? No. A foreign individual can buy a flat, a house or a commercial unit without one. A purchase does not, however, give you a right to reside, which is handled separately. Can I buy farmland or forest as a foreigner? Land and forests follow separate rules, and restrictions have varied with the buyer and the use of the land. Ask a Czech lawyer before making any offer. Is it easier to buy through a company? It is possible, but it changes the legal and tax position considerably and is a matter for a lawyer and a tax adviser, not a shortcut. Can someone sign for me if I am abroad? Yes, through a representative with a power of attorney, but it must be in the right form and is best prepared by a Czech lawyer or notary. Where can I check who owns a flat? In the Cadastre of Real Estate. The online view run by ČÚZK is free. A first step Before you fall for a particular flat, open the free online view of the Cadastre on the ČÚZK website and search for any address. It takes a few minutes and shows you what an ownership record looks like. Then book an hour with a Czech lawyer who works with foreign buyers and ask for the list of documents they would need from you. This is a general explainer, not legal, tax or mortgage advice.
